## Managing Firewalls, Access Control, and Compliance Across Distributed HPC Architectures


829 agency


October 11, 2026


Every additional cloud your engineering teams touch is another firewall configuration, another identity system, another compliance boundary that has to be kept consistent with the other two. It’s manageable when you’re running on one cloud. It gets exponentially harder with every cloud you add, because each provider’s native security tools were built to secure that provider’s environment, not to work in concert with the others.


The organizations that pass audits without a scramble aren’t the ones with the most security tools. They’re the ones with a consistent HPC storage architecture and security policy that behaves the same way no matter which cloud a workload happens to be running on.


## **Why Security Policy Drifts Apart Across Clouds**

Left unmanaged, security policy drifts because each cloud has its own native firewall rules, its own identity and access management system, and its own logging format. A team needs a one-off exception in one cloud, gets it, and six months later nobody remembers why that exception exists or whether it’s still needed. Multiply that across AWS, Azure, and GCP, and multiply it again across every project, and you end up with a patchwork that nobody could fully explain if an auditor asked.


## **What Consistent Compliance Looks Like in a Multi-Cloud HPC Environment**


Consistent compliance means access controls, encryption, and auditability are enforced the same way regardless of which cloud a workload runs on. For organizations working under frameworks like SOC 2, ISO, ITAR, or FedRAMP, this matters directly: an auditor shouldn’t need a separate explanation of how compliance works in each cloud, because the answer should be the same everywhere.


## **The Core Controls IT Needs to Standardize**


Three areas do most of the work in closing the gap between fragmented, cloud-by-cloud security and something an auditor can actually verify.


### **Access Controls and Identity**


Standardized identity and single sign-on give you one place to manage who has access to what, instead of three separate identity systems that can silently drift out of sync with each other over time.


### **Encryption and Auditability**


Built-in encryption and a full audit trail aren’t optional for regulated engineering workloads. The question isn’t whether you have them, it’s whether they work the same way regardless of which cloud the workload happens to be running on.


### **Hardware and Software Curation**


Limiting engineers to a pre-vetted set of approved configurations closes off an entire category of compliance risk before it becomes a question anyone has to answer. If the only available options are already compliant, there’s nothing to audit for exceptions.


## **How Rescale Standardizes Security Across Distributed HPC**


Rescale’s platform is built with SOC 2, ISO, ITAR, and FedRAMP-ready infrastructure as a baseline, not an add-on. Encryption, access controls, and full auditability are built in and applied consistently regardless of which cloud a workload runs on, and hardware and software curation limits engineers to pre-approved, compliant configurations from the start.


## **Building an Audit-Ready Multi-Cloud HPC Environment**


Before your next audit finds the drift for you, run your own access-control and firewall-rule audit across every cloud in use. Compare what’s actually configured against what your policy says should be configured, and you’ll usually find the gaps before anyone external does.


If you want help mapping your current multi-cloud security posture against a consistent standard, Rescale’s team can walk through what that looks like on our platform.
